research_area: namespace/partition/isolation patterns for memory and vector stores in multi-agent platforms
constraint_context: meept: pure-Go single-daemon self-hosted agent platform, SQLite-backed storage, daemon-wide memory subsystem shared by named agents; no heavyweight external services; needs per-agent/per-group isolation.

pinecone_namespaces.model: An index contains namespaces; every upsert/query targets exactly one namespace. One namespace per tenant is Pinecone's recommended multi-tenancy pattern. In the serverless architecture each namespace is stored separately, giving physical isolation, no noisy neighbors, cheap tenant offboarding (delete namespace), and lower query cost than metadata filtering (query cost scales with namespace size, not total index size). Queries can never span namespaces; cross-tenant search requires the (discouraged) metadata-filtering pattern or client-side merge.
pinecone_namespaces.license: Proprietary managed cloud service; no self-hosting.
pinecone_namespaces.go_integration: Hosted REST/gRPC API; official Go client exists (pinecone-io/pinecone-go), but it is always a remote cloud call.
pinecone_namespaces.maturity: Production, commercial SaaS; namespaces-per-index limits scale with plan (100 Starter to 1,000,000 Enterprise).
pinecone_namespaces.fit_for_meept: Poor. Violates the no-external-services constraint outright. The design lesson is transferable though: hard per-tenant scope enforced at every read/write boundary, plus O(1) tenant deletion, is exactly the property to reproduce in SQLite.

qdrant.model: Qdrant documents three tenant-isolation strategies: (1) Partition by payload - a tenant-identifying payload field (e.g. user_id) indexed with is_tenant=true so same-tenant points co-locate for sequential reads; recommended default for many small tenants. (2) Separate collections per tenant - explicitly discouraged: each collection has resource overhead, clusters cap at 1000 collections by default, and Qdrant's own guidance says only use them for a few tenants with legal/compliance-grade isolation requirements. (3) User-defined sharding (v1.7+) and tiered multitenancy - dedicated shard per large tenant, shared shard for small ones. Payload filtering already guarantees query-level isolation; separate collections are an exception for compliance, not the default.
qdrant.license: Apache-2.0 (verified from qdrant/qdrant LICENSE and Cargo.toml). Self-hostable, written in Rust. Go client qdrant/go-client is also Apache-2.0 (pkg.go.dev v1.20.1).
qdrant.go_integration: Official Go client library (github.com/qdrant/go-client, gRPC-based) - but it is a client to a separate Rust server process; there is no embedded mode.
qdrant.fit_for_meept: Technically clean (Apache-2.0, first-class Go client, payload-filter isolation maps 1:1 to per-agent scoping) but it is exactly the 'separate server' the constraint excludes: another binary to run, back up, version, and secure, for a daemon whose vector workload is likely small. Viable only as an optional opt-in backend if meept ever outgrows SQLite-scale vectors. Note: SQLite itself can serve modest vector search (vec0/sqlite-vec extension or brute-force cosine over a namespaced table), which keeps everything in the one file.

sqlite_row_level_isolation.model: SQLite has NO native row-level security (no RLS, no per-user roles). Verified replacement patterns: (1) Application-level WHERE scoping - every query on a shared table carries 'WHERE namespace/agent_id = ?' via a bound host parameter; the SQLite forum's own guidance says if users cannot submit arbitrary SQL, implement it at the application level with a host parameter for the current user. This is the dominant pattern. (2) sqlite3_set_authorizer callbacks - a compile-time (prepare-time) hook that can allow/deny/ignore per action code (SQLITE_READ/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE...) at TABLE and COLUMN granularity. It cannot filter rows: SQLITE_IGNORE on SQLITE_READ nulls a column, it does not hide rows; authorization happens only during sqlite3_prepare (plus re-prepare after schema changes), never per-row during step. It is a defense-in-depth tool against injected SQL, not an isolation mechanism. (3) Views + authorizer - expose a scoped view (CREATE VIEW ... WHERE owner = current_user()) and use the authorizer to deny direct access to the base table, with INSTEAD OF triggers for writes; recommended on the SQLite forum for the untrusted-SQL case. (4) Raise(ABORT) BEFORE triggers checking an application-defined current_user() SQL function. (5) Extensions/add-ons: sqlite-vec (vec0) supports metadata/partition keys (e.g. partition_key / chunk metadata filters) so vector data can be partitioned inside the same SQLite file; nothing RLS-like exists in core.
sqlite_row_level_isolation.license: SQLite is public domain. sqlite-vec is MIT/Apache-2.0 dual (verify before vendoring - not re-verified in this pass).
sqlite_row_level_isolation.go_integration: Native: modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go, no cgo) and mattn/go-sqlite3 both expose the authorizer if needed; sqlite-vec has a Go binding. Namespaced tables need nothing beyond SQL.
sqlite_row_level_isolation.maturity: SQLite is the most deployed DB in the world; the pattern (app-enforced scoping) is what effectively every embedded-SQLite application does.
sqlite_row_level_isolation.fit_for_meept: Excellent - this IS the sound pattern for meept. Because the daemon is the only SQL speaker (no untrusted SQL reaches the engine), application-enforced scoping is sufficient: a required agent_id/group_id column (or per-agent namespaced tables, e.g. memory_<agent> or a shared table with a NOT NULL scope column + covering index), bound parameters on every statement, and a repository layer that structurally cannot issue unscoped queries. Defense-in-depth additions if desired: CHECK constraints, and an authorizer callback only if there is any future risk of agent-supplied SQL reaching prepare. Caveat to document: isolation is only as strong as the code discipline around it - an omitted WHERE clause silently leaks, so enforce it centrally (one scoped-query builder, no raw table access outside the memory package). This mirrors Pinecone's namespace model (every op names its scope) at zero infra cost, and is precisely what Mem0/Letta do internally anyway (they are Postgres/SQLite + app-level scoping under the hood).

mem0.model: Entity-scoped memory: every memory write (add) and read (search/get_all/delete_all) is tagged with identifiers - user_id (persistent persona/account), agent_id (distinct agent persona), run_id (short-lived session/flow), and app_id (tenant/app surface, PLATFORM ONLY; OSS supports user_id/agent_id/run_id only). Reads accept filter objects with AND/OR/NOT; unmentioned entities are unconstrained. Notable semantics: on the default extraction path a fact is attributed to whoever stated it - a record carries user_id XOR agent_id (app_id/run_id always carried), so an AND filter on both returns nothing; use OR or direct import (infer=False) for both-set records. Multi-agent group chat requires explicitly calling add() per participant - scope is never inferred.
mem0.license: Apache-2.0 for the OSS core (verified from mem0ai/mem0 repo LICENSE badge/readme as of research date). Open-core: hosted Platform adds app_id/orgs/projects, Graph Memory, decay, etc. License-status caveat, verified: the license has NOT changed to a non-OSI license, but Mem0 v3 (April 2026) REMOVED graph-store support from the open-source SDK and moved graph dashboards to the hosted Platform - a feature-removal open-core event, not a relicensing. Third-party risk assessments flag structural relicensing risk (single VC-backed vendor). Pin a version if depending on it.
mem0.separate_service: Depends: Python library (pip install mem0ai) runs in-process but needs an LLM + embedder + a vector store (its own external dependency); self-hosted server mode is a Docker API server backed by PostgreSQL+pgvector. Either way, from a Go program it is a separate service (HTTP) or not usable as a library at all.
mem0.go_integration: No in-process Go library exists (OSS core is Python; JS SDK for platform). Official Go SDK github.com/mem0ai/mem0-go is a thin HTTP client for the hosted Platform API; community clients (plexusone/mem0-go MIT, Alcova-AI/mem0-go) also target the REST API and can point at a self-hosted server via base URL.
mem0.maturity: Very popular (67k+ stars) but young and fast-moving; open-core with recent feature removals from OSS.
mem0.fit_for_meept: Poor as a dependency (Python/Postgres stack or a remote API), but its identifier model (user_id/agent_id/run_id + AND/OR filters, scope never inferred) is the right vocabulary for meept's memory API design. Adopt the taxonomy, not the software.

zep.model: Per-user temporal knowledge graphs: every user gets a user graph (created with the user) integrating context across all their threads; threads do NOT partition the graph - they integrate into one user-level picture, and thread.get_context returns the most relevant user-level context. Shared/domain context goes in separately-addressable Context Graphs (graph_uuid). Isolation is by account and project boundaries plus policy-based access control; user deletion cascades to all threads and the entire user graph (RTBF).
zep.license: Split, verified: Zep Community Edition (the self-hostable memory server, formerly Apache-2.0) is DEPRECATED and no longer supported - the repo remains under Apache 2.0 but receives no updates. The company's open-source focus is Graphiti (the temporal-graph framework powering Zep), Apache-2.0. Zep the product is now Cloud or enterprise BYOC only. Graphiti requires you to bring a graph database (Neo4j, FalkorDB, or Amazon Neptune).
zep.go_integration: Graphiti is Python/TypeScript (framework + MCP server); the Zep platform ships Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs - but as HTTP clients to the cloud/BYOC service. Self-hosting Graphiti means running Python plus a graph database.
zep.maturity: Commercially mature (Zep Cloud), OSS path (Graphiti) active but framework-level: tenancy, ingestion, and access control are explicitly YOUR build, per Zep's own README.
zep.fit_for_meept: Poor. Deprecated self-host option, cloud-first product, and even the OSS Graphiti path drags in a graph database and a Python service. Design takeaway: per-subject graphs that merge thread-level context upward (thread -> agent -> group) and cascade-delete per subject are worth copying in SQLite.

letta.model: Per-agent memory as first-class DB state: each agent has a persisted AgentState whose context window is 'compiled' from DB state at request time. Memory is structured into memory blocks - labeled (human/persona/knowledge...), size-limited, individually persisted string units with block_id, editable by the agent via tools or by developers via API/ADE; blocks can be read-only. Multi-agent shared memory is a headline feature: multiple agents attach the SAME block (shared knowledge base, sleep-time compute agents updating a primary agent's memory). Identities/identity_ids attach agents to users for per-user separation in a multi-tenant server.
letta.go_integration: No Go library - Letta is TypeScript/Python (repo now centers on letta-code; the Python V1 API server is archived to the 'archive' branch and the Docker/Postgres server surface is retired). Integration is via the Letta App Server (self-hosted, 'letta server', now websocket/HTTP with capability-token auth) or Letta Cloud, from any language's HTTP/WS client. Historically the server used PostgreSQL for state.
letta.maturity: High (25k+ stars, commercial company, active development), but the deployment surface churned significantly in 2025-2026 (Python server EOL, Docker image repurposed).
letta.fit_for_meept: Not adoptable (external server, TS/Python stack), but the memory-block architecture is the most directly portable IDEA in this whole survey: per-agent state = ordered, size-capped, labeled blocks persisted in SQLite, addressable by id, optionally SHARED between agents by block reference (which solves meept's per-group memory requirement elegantly - a group memory is just a block attached to multiple agents), with the context window compiled from blocks at prompt time. This is implementable in meept's existing SQLite file with zero new services.

synthesis_recommendation.verdict: Namespaced tables in the existing SQLite file + application-enforced scoping is a sound, industry-consistent pattern for meept - it is what the embedded path of every surveyed system does internally (Mem0 = tagged rows + filters; Letta = per-agent block rows + shared block refs; Qdrant/Pinecone = scope key carried on every operation), and SQLite's own forum guidance prescribes app-level WHERE scoping when the application is the only SQL speaker.
synthesis_recommendation.concrete_pattern: 1) A required NOT NULL scope column (agent_id, plus optional group_id) on every memory/vector row with a covering index (scope, created_at) - 'Pinecone namespace' semantics: every read/write must name its scope, tenant deletion becomes one indexed DELETE. 2) Shared memory for groups via Letta-style shared blocks: rows referenced by multiple agents (agent_block join table) instead of copying. 3) Enforce scoping centrally in the memory repository layer; forbid raw table access elsewhere (meept already has internal/memory with this seam). 4) Vector search in-file: brute-force cosine or sqlite-vec partition keys at meept's scale; keep an optional Qdrant backend (Apache-2.0, official Go client) behind the same interface only if scale ever demands it. 5) Optional defense-in-depth: sqlite3_set_authorizer if agent-supplied SQL can ever reach prepare (table/column level only - it cannot do row filtering).
synthesis_recommendation.anti_patterns: Separate collection/table per agent as a default (Qdrant explicitly calls this an anti-pattern past a few hundred tenants; per-agent SQLite tables forfeit cross-agent queries and shared blocks); relying on the SQLite authorizer for row isolation (it cannot); adopting Mem0/Zep/Letta servers to get 'memory isolation' (each buys a service to get a feature meept can implement in ~a table schema); metadata-only filtering in a shared vector index with no scope column (Pinecone's documented cost/perf anti-pattern: filters scan everything).
